package_info.package_versions: all published versions (since at least Dec 4, 2023)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages abuse the npm registry by storing and distributing large, non-software media files (movies, video clips, and associated metadata), violating the platform's terms of service and potentially facilitating the distribution of pirated content. This undermines the integrity and intended use of the software supply chain.

execution_context.trigger: at package publish and install time
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (multiple .ts files, e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At package publish and install time, the package includes large binary .ts files (video clips) in the published artifact, enabling the download and reconstruction of full movies from the npm registry.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Software packages are expected to contain source code and related assets, not large video files. The presence of multi-gigabyte video data is a clear abuse of the registry.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages contain code and small assets necessary for the software to function. Here, the package is used as a file hosting mechanism for pirated or unauthorized media.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include small demo videos or images for documentation, but not full-length movies or large media libraries.
key_indicators: Presence of large .ts (MPEG-TS) files in package root
Package size (~54.5 MB each) far exceeds typical npm package size
No actual executable code or software functionality

execution_context.trigger: at package publish and install time
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (JSON files, e.g., comments.json)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At package publish and install time, the package includes JSON files containing time-synced user comments, likely extracted from online video platforms, as metadata for the included video clips.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Including large, unrelated metadata files (such as time-synced comments) is not typical for npm packages and further indicates the package's use as a media distribution mechanism.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages may include configuration or metadata files, but not large datasets of user comments tied to pirated media.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use might include subtitles or small metadata for demo videos, but not for full-length pirated content.
key_indicators: Presence of large JSON files with time-synced comments
Metadata unrelated to any software functionality

attack_chain.action: Attacker splits a movie into multiple video clips (.ts files) and prepares associated metadata (JSON comments).
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation of package artifacts for upload

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes multiple npm packages (wlwz-*) each containing a segment of the movie and associated metadata.
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages are available for download from npm registry

attack_chain.action: Users (or automated scripts) download all related packages to reconstruct the full movie and metadata.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution and consumption of pirated media via npm

behavioral_signatures: npm packages containing large binary files with .ts extension
Packages with no executable code or software functionality
Packages with large JSON files containing time-synced comments or metadata
file_indicators: *.ts files in package root (not TypeScript, but MPEG-TS video)
comments.json or similar large metadata files
network_indicators: No direct network indicators (malware does not exfiltrate data or contact C2 servers), but bulk download of wlwz-* packages may indicate abuse
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Flag npm packages that contain large binary files with .ts extensions (excluding TypeScript), especially when package size exceeds typical thresholds (e.g., >10MB) and there is no corresponding executable code. Monitor for packages with large JSON metadata files unrelated to software functionality. Bulk downloads of similarly named packages (e.g., wlwz-*) may indicate attempts to reconstruct pirated media. Automated scanning should alert on packages with high storage-to-code ratio and non-software content.
